extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics students, and general readers interested in the philosophy, sociology, and practice of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for judging mathematical work, mathematical intuition, models, and novel claims (including unsolicited or heterodox submissions), and for understanding why mathematics 'works' in applied contexts. Covers community acceptance, sources of discovery (individual vs culture), and proper modeling choices (e.g., when to add).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge requires symbolic expressibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "Knowledge, as I understand it in the technical sense, implies that it can be expressed in symbols."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats technical knowledge as that which can be expressed symbolically; by analogy, a writer or a piece of music 'models' an evoked state. This suggests a criterion for technical knowledge or mathematical understanding: can it be formulated in appropriate symbolic language?

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition as stored experience, useful but fallible
rubrics_metrics.description: "What is scientific or mathematical intuition? 'Intuition is an expression of experience. Stored experience.' ... 'To what extent can one be deceived by intuition? This occurs not infrequently.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition is valuable (guides model choice and quick judgements) but can mislead. Use intuition to generate hypotheses or compare models, but always test and verify formally; expect individual differences in pace and reliability of intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of crank or amateur submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical unsolicited/sensational submissions often come from amateurs with 'very little training', poor understanding of the problem, and an 'imperfect notion of just what a mathematical proof is and how it operates.' They may include lengthy autobiographies and unrelated grandiose claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are anti-patterns that usually justify quick dismissal: sensational claims (e.g., solves Fermat), lack of clear understanding of definitions/problems, poor structure or opaque exposition, and extraneous personal or grandiose material. Nonetheless, do not rely solely on surface cues—some obscure submissions may hide genuine insight (Ramanujan example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of mathematical output and community responses
rubrics_metrics.description: There is work which is wrong and promptly corrected; work dismissed without examination; work so obscure that it is ignored but may later be rediscovered; heterodox work which is boycotted (e.g., Cantor); and correct work that is ignored for lack of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify novel or heterodox work into these categories when deciding response. Recognize that the community's selection mechanisms are imperfect and historically contingent; acceptance or rejection is not fully formalizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triage criteria for novel claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with a purported solution to a famous problem, one should assess the author's understanding of the problem, clarity of exposition, presence of rigorous proof, and plausibility (consistency with known results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend quick initial time checking whether the submission addresses the right problem and whether key logical steps are justified; look for clear counterexamples to obvious flaws. High-cost, high-payoff cases (e.g., a credible short proof) may warrant deeper examination. Historical counterexamples (Rademacher error; Ramanujan's pearls) illustrate both false alarms and missed genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: No formal rule for what mathematicizing accepts
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the final analysis, there can be no formalization of what is right and how we know it is right, what is accepted, and what the mechanism for acceptance is." (paraphrase of Hermann Weyl)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect subjectivity and historical contingency in judgments of mathematical importance and correctness; use community mechanisms (peer review, replication, clarity) but acknowledge they won't capture every future-relevant contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing sources of discovery: individual vs culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Two doctrines: (1) the individual (great geniuses are primary), and (2) the culture (Zeitgeist/social forces bring forth discovery). Neither extreme suffices; reconciliation includes time-scale distinctions and James' view that community and individual mutually support discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the origin or importance of a result, consider both individual creativity and wider cultural, institutional, and temporal contexts: short-term breakthroughs may be individual-driven; long-term trends reflect cultural factors. Look for enabling institutions, training, and zeitgeist as well as individual talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platonism versus conventionalism about why mathematics works
rubrics_metrics.description: Platonist view: mathematics exists independently ('out there') and we 'listen to the universe.' Conventionalist/model view: mathematics consists of structures we create and then try to fit the world into these patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction affects evaluation of models: Platonists may seek 'true' mathematical descriptions; conventionalists emphasize model-building, fit, and usefulness. Be explicit about which stance informs your modelling and interpretive choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model-selection criteria: simplicity, fruitfulness, predictive success
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical models are judged by their success in mimicking or predicting behavior; qualities like simplicity and fruitfulness matter. There is no absolute 'philosophical truth'—competing models are assessed by practical criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing or evaluating a model, ask: Does it simplify without losing essential behavior? Does it generate new useful insights or predictions? Does it match empirical data? Be willing to replace models when they fail these tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three aspects of an operation (example: addition) — algorithm, formal laws, applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition has (1) algorithmic aspect (how to perform it), (2) formal laws it obeys (commutativity, associativity, etc.), and (3) applications — under what circumstances does one add? The third is often the hardest and most context-dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In applied problems, carefully distinguish computation from modelling: verify that adding is the correct operation for the context (unit consistency, meaning of summed quantities). Use concrete checks (units, conservation laws, limiting cases) to validate the modelling choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware inappropriate summation and ad hoc 'figures of merit' in applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete examples show failures of naive addition: retail discounts (tuna price), pricing of incommensurate goods (Mona Lisa duplicates), ad hoc credit/rating systems summing heterogeneous attributes, mixing volumes with different densities, and combining work rates incorrectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronted with a summed score or aggregated measure, check whether components are commensurate and whether addition preserves meaning. Consider alternative models (vector pricing, weighted indices with justified scales, harmonic sums for rates). Recognize the arbitrary/ad-hoc nature of many 'figures of merit' and require justification for the aggregation rule.
